rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.3 - two-year (2018-2019) replicated field experiments on maize at Zhengzhou (FI, DI, RF) and TandoJam (F100, F75, F50), with measured soil water, soil N, LAI, dry matter and grain yield used to calibrate and validate the WHCNS model. Q2: Section 3.2 and Table 4 - at Zhengzhou drip irrigation used 90 mm vs 240 mm under flood over two years (62.5% less water, recorded by separate water meters); WUE under DI was 3.4 and 3.2 kg/m3 vs 2.6 and 2.7 for FI (order DI > FI > RF); Abstract reports WUE improved up to 24.5%. Q4: Section 3.3 and Table 4 - the model (validated against measured soil water content) gives soil evaporation of ~147 mm under DI vs ~196 mm under FI (33% higher under flood) with similar transpiration, plus negligible drainage and runoff under DI vs ~20 mm drainage under FI, i.e. the pathway of the water saving/WUE gain is quantified.
rows.notes: Drip vs flood was tested only at the Zhengzhou site on 130 m2 plots (TandoJam compared flood deficit levels, not drip), so no multi-site or above-plot evidence for the drip claim. Water saving is directly measured; WUE relies on simulated ET (model validated on soil water, not on ET), so no independent second method. No requirement conditions for the drip effect are stated from own findings (cost barrier in TandoJam is cited from Tunio et al.). No limitations of the result are discussed. Table 4 reports per-year values but no SD, CI or uncertainty propagation; RMSE/d/r are validation statistics only.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.3 - own two-year replicated field experiments with measured grain yield, dry matter and LAI at both sites. Q2: Section 3.2 and Fig. 3 - at Zhengzhou drip irrigation gave a significantly (p<0.05) higher two-year total grain yield of 22,449 kg/ha vs 20,434 kg/ha under farmer flood irrigation (9.8% increase) and 70.7% above rainfed; Conclusions state DI significantly improved yield compared to full flood irrigation. Q4: Sections 2.1, 2.3, 3.2 and Table 5 - root-zone soil water content was measured weekly and held at 50-80% of field capacity under DI, dry matter and LAI were measured at growth stages and were higher under DI, and simulated crop N uptake was 8.9% higher under DI; authors attribute the yield gain to this maintained soil water, vigorous growth and biomass accumulation.
rows.notes: Drip vs flood yield comparison exists only at one site (Zhengzhou, sandy clay loam, one cultivar), on 130 m2 plots. Simulated yield is calibrated on the measured yield, so it is not an independent method. The mechanistic step of topsoil oversaturation/lack of air under flood is asserted with a citation, not measured; Q4 'yes' rests on measured soil water and biomass/LAI, which is a somewhat generous reading. No conditions stated as requirements for the drip yield effect; no limitations of the result given; only LSD significance at p<0.05, no SD/CI reported in text or tables.

notes: Full text appears complete (abstract through references). Fig. S1 (supplementary) not available; Fig. 3 bars cannot be inspected for error bars, so Q9 answered 'no' on the basis of the tables and text. Water balance components (ET, drainage, runoff) and N fates are model outputs from a model validated on measured soil water, N, LAI, dry matter and yield; irrigation amounts and grain yield are directly measured.
